Synopsis:
    A global bond selloff is underway, with the US 10-year yield breaking above 4.75% for the first time since January of the prior year. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh partially restored credibility at Jackson Hole by reaffirming the 2% inflation target and signaling willingness to hike in September, but markets remain skeptical of follow-through. The selloff is global — France, Germany, and Japan yields are at multi-decade highs. Geopolitical pressure (US-Iran war, oil above $90) adds to risk-off pressure on equities. A G20 finance summit adds a wildcard via debate on yuan undervaluation (estimated 20–35%) and a potential Plaza Accord-style currency agreement.

Q01. Is the content's main message on the US economy, US yields, US interest rates?
Relevance: YES (the article centers on the US bond market selloff, Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish pivot, and the September rate hike expectations)

Sentiment: 70 (meaningfully hawkish — 10Y above 4.75%, short-end yields spiking, September hike being priced in post-Warsh Jackson Hole speech; geopolitical and oil price pressures compound the inflationary/hawkish backdrop; however residual uncertainty around Warsh's execution prevents a full hawkish reading)
